  rw [map_le_iff_le_comap] at hx hy

applications.title: Certify an infinite monomial family
applications.inputs: In the real polynomial vector space R[X], take v_n=X^n for every natural n.

steps.text: Define the induced outer mass of an event S as the supremum of finite subsums with indices inside S.
If S is finite, its own subsum is among these subsums. Every subsum over a finite subset F of S is at most the sum over S, since the omitted masses are nonnegative.
Thus the supremum is at least and at most the sum over S, and the two are equal.
For S empty, the only subsum is 0, so the formula still holds. This argument applies to every finite event without a sigma-algebra assumption.

steps.text: Suppose the outer mass of S is 0. For any a in S, its singleton subsum p(a) is at most the outer mass of S, so p(a)=0.
The zero-outside-support lemma gives a outside the support for every a in S. Thus S is disjoint from the support.
Conversely, if S is disjoint from the support, every p(a) with a in S is zero. Every finite subsum inside S is then zero.
Their supremum, the induced outer mass of S, is zero. This argument applies to arbitrary S, including an empty event.

results.name: An event has mass 1 exactly when it contains the support
results.statement: For a probability mass function p and any subset S, its induced outer probability is 1 if and only if S contains the support.
hypotheses: p is a probability mass function on A.
S is any subset of A.
Outer probability is the sum of p over S.

prerequisites.reason: Support containment makes every omitted mass vanish.

source.excerpt:
theorem toOuterMeasure_apply_eq_one_iff : p.toOuterMeasure s = 1 ↔ p.support ⊆ s := by
  refine (p.toOuterMeasure_apply s).symm ▸ ⟨fun h a hap => ?_, fun h => ?_⟩
  · refine by_contra fun hs => ne_of_lt ?_ (h.trans p.tsum_coe.symm)
    have hs' : s.indicator p a = 0 := Set.indicator_apply_eq_zero.2 fun hs' => False.elim <| hs hs'
    have hsa : s.indicator p a < p a := hs'.symm ▸ (p.apply_pos_iff a).2 hap
    exact ENNReal.tsum_lt_tsum (p.tsum_coe_indicator_ne_top s)
      (fun x => Set.indicator_apply_le fun _ => le_rfl) hsa
  · classical suffices ∀ (x) (_ : x ∉ s), p x = 0 from
      _root_.trans (tsum_congr
        fun a => (Set.indicator_apply s p a).trans
          (ite_eq_left_iff.2 <| symm ∘ this a)) p.tsum_coe
    exact fun a ha => (p.apply_eq_zero_iff a).2 <| Set.notMem_subset h ha

results.name: Set.prod_eq_prod_iff
results.statement: A times B equals A1 times B1 if and only if A=A1 and B=B1, or both products have an empty factor.
hypotheses: U,V are arbitrary sets. A,A1,A2 are subsets of U. B,B1,B2 are subsets of V. Empty factors are permitted unless excluded below.

proof.verification: complete readable proof; agent review required; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Equal factors give equal products, and an empty factor makes either product empty. These facts prove the reverse implication.

Suppose the common product is nonempty. Both factors on each side are nonempty. First-coordinate projection gives A=A1. For any y in B, choose x in A. The product equality puts (x,y) in A1 times B1, so y belongs to B1. Conversely, choose x in A1 for any y in B1 to prove y in B. Hence B=B1.
If the common product is empty, the product nonemptiness lemma implies that each product has an empty factor. This completes all cases.

prerequisites.reason: The proof detects empty products through their factors.
Coordinate projections recover each nonempty factor. The second-coordinate proof is identical after exchanging the coordinate names.

source.excerpt:
theorem prod_eq_prod_iff :
    s ×ˢ t = s₁ ×ˢ t₁ ↔ s = s₁ ∧ t = t₁ ∨ (s = ∅ ∨ t = ∅) ∧ (s₁ = ∅ ∨ t₁ = ∅) := by
  symm
  rcases eq_empty_or_nonempty (s ×ˢ t) with h | h
  · simp_rw [h, @eq_comm _ ∅, prod_eq_empty_iff, prod_eq_empty_iff.mp h, true_and,
      or_iff_right_iff_imp]
    rintro ⟨rfl, rfl⟩
    exact prod_eq_empty_iff.mp h
  rw [prod_eq_prod_iff_of_nonempty h]
  rw [nonempty_iff_ne_empty, Ne, prod_eq_empty_iff] at h
  simp_rw [h, false_and, or_false]

results.name: Function.bijective_iff_existsUnique
results.statement: A function f:A->B is bijective if and only if every b in B has exactly 1 preimage in A.
hypotheses: A,B,C are arbitrary sets. Every function has its displayed domain and codomain.

proof.verification: complete readable proof; agent review required; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Bijectivity gives a preimage by surjectivity. Any two preimages agree by injectivity, so the preimage is unique.
Conversely, existence of each preimage is surjectivity. If f(x)=f(y), x,y are preimages of the same point. Uniqueness gives x=y, so f is injective.

source.excerpt:
theorem bijective_iff_existsUnique (f : α → β) : Bijective f ↔ ∀ b : β, ∃! a : α, f a = b :=
  ⟨fun hf b ↦
      let ⟨a, ha⟩ := hf.surjective b
      ⟨a, ha, fun _ ha' ↦ hf.injective (ha'.trans ha.symm)⟩,
    fun he ↦ ⟨fun {_a a'} h ↦ (he (f a')).unique h rfl, fun b ↦ (he b).exists⟩⟩

results.statement: In a lattice, meet(a,b)<join(a,b) if and only if a is not equal to b.
hypotheses: L is a lattice. The symbols join and meet denote its least upper bound and greatest lower bound operations.

proof.verification: complete readable proof; agent review required; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: If a=b, both meet and join equal a, so strict inequality is false.
Always meet(a,b)<=a,b<=join(a,b). If meet and join are equal, these inequalities squeeze both a,b to that common value by antisymmetry. Thus a=b.

results.name: mem_closure_iff
results.statement: A point x lies in closure(A) if and only if every open neighborhood of x meets A.
hypotheses: X is any topological space. A,B are subsets of X. Empty subsets are permitted.

steps.text: If an open neighborhood O of x missed A, then its closed complement would contain A. Minimality would put closure(A) inside that complement, so x could not lie in the closure.

applications.title: Approximate nonnegative reals by rational squares
applications.inputs: Take the dense inclusion f:Q->R and g:R->[0,infinity), g(x)=x^2. The codomain has its subspace topology.
applications.hypotheses: Assume the standard density of Q in R. Squaring is continuous, and every nonnegative real is a square.

steps.text: At a real a, |x^2-a^2|=|x-a||x+a|. If |x-a|<1, then |x+a|<2|a|+1. Choosing delta=min(1,epsilon/(2|a|+1)) proves continuity of squaring.
For each t>=0, the values at 0 and t+1 bracket t, because 0<=t<(t+1)^2. The intermediate value theorem gives a real x with x^2=t. Thus g is surjective and has dense range.
The dense-composition theorem proves that rational squares are dense in the nonnegative reals. Rational approximations 1.4,1.41 and 1.414 give the following concrete values near 2.
The rational 1.41 has square 1.9881, which is closer to 2 than the first square.
The rational 1.414 has square 1.999396. The exact difference from 2 is 0.000604.

applications.conclusion: Every neighborhood of every nonnegative real contains a rational square. The displayed exact computations give 3 examples near 2.

results.name: abs_pow_eq_one
results.statement: For a real a and positive natural n, abs(a^n)=1 if and only if abs(a)=1.
hypotheses: All displayed scalars are real numbers. Division by 0 follows the source convention x/0=0 only where explicitly permitted.
n is a positive natural number.

steps.text: Put t=abs(a)>=0. The absolute-power lemma gives abs(a^n)=t^n.

If 0<=t<1, induction gives 0<=t^n<1 for n>=1. The base n=1 holds. If u=t^n is in [0,1), then 0<=ut<=u<1. If t>1, the base t^1>1 holds, and u>1 implies ut>u>1. Thus every positive power stays strictly below or strictly above 1 in these two cases.
Thus t^n=1 forces t=1 by trichotomy. Conversely, t=1 gives t^n=1.

prerequisites.reason: The power identity reduces the claim to a nonnegative real power.

lemma abs_pow_eq_one (a : α) (h : n ≠ 0) : |a ^ n| = 1 ↔ |a| = 1 := by
  convert pow_left_inj₀ (abs_nonneg a) zero_le_one h
  exacts [(pow_abs _ _).symm, (one_pow _).symm]

hypotheses: G is a group with a seminorm N:G->[0,infinity). It satisfies N(1)=0, N(g inverse)=N(g), and N(gh)<=N(g)+N(h). The operation need not commute.
n is any natural number, including 0.

proof.verification: complete readable proof; agent review required; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: For n=0, the power is 1 and both sides are 0. Suppose the bound holds at n.
Since g^(n+1)=g^n g, the triangle axiom gives N(g^(n+1))<=N(g^n)+N(g)<=n N(g)+N(g)=(n+1)N(g). Induction finishes the proof.

source.excerpt:
lemma norm_pow_le_mul_norm : ∀ {n : ℕ}, ‖a ^ n‖ ≤ n * ‖a‖
  | 0 => by simp
  | n + 1 => by simpa [pow_succ, add_mul] using norm_mul_le_of_le' norm_pow_le_mul_norm le_rfl

results.statement: In a seminormed abelian additive group, the norm of a finite multiset sum is at most the sum of the norms.

The induction hypothesis bounds the last norm by the sum of the norms in M. Adding N(x) gives the required sum for the enlarged multiset.

results.name: norm_prod_le
results.statement: In a seminormed abelian multiplicative group, the seminorm of a finite product is at most the sum of the seminorms of its factors.
hypotheses: G is a group with a seminorm N:G->[0,infinity). It satisfies N(1)=0, N(g inverse)=N(g), and N(gh)<=N(g)+N(h). The operation need not commute.

Remove one factor g_j. The triangle axiom bounds the seminorm of the product by N(g_j) plus the seminorm of the remaining product.

results.statement: For a map f:X->V into a normed additive group, the real function N composed with f has compact support if and only if f has compact support.

results.name: linearIndependent_of_ne_zero_of_inner_eq_zero
results.statement: Every pairwise orthogonal family of nonzero vectors in a real or complex inner product space is linearly independent.
hypotheses: V is a real or complex inner product space. The first slot is conjugate-linear and the second is linear. The norm satisfies N(x)^2=<x,x>.
The norm separates 0. I is any index set. v_i is nonzero for every i, and <v_i,v_j>=0 whenever i is not equal to j.

proof.verification: complete readable proof; agent review required; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Consider any finitely supported relation sum_i c_i v_i=0. Fix an index j in its finite support.
Take the inner product with v_j in the first slot. Repeated right-slot linearity expands the finite sum. Orthogonality removes every term except c_j<v_j,v_j>, so this product is 0.
Since v_j is nonzero, the zero-diagonal criterion gives <v_j,v_j> nonzero. Division in the scalar field gives c_j=0.
This holds for every index in the support. All other coefficients vanish by definition of support. Therefore every finite relation is trivial, which is linear independence.

prerequisites.reason: Each nonzero vector has a nonzero diagonal inner product.

source.excerpt:
theorem linearIndependent_of_ne_zero_of_inner_eq_zero {ι : Type*} {v : ι → E} (hz : ∀ i, v i ≠ 0)
    (ho : Pairwise fun i j => ⟪v i, v j⟫ = 0) : LinearIndependent 𝕜 v := by
  rw [linearIndependent_iff']
  intro s g hg i hi
  have h' : g i * ⟪v i, v i⟫ = ⟪v i, ∑ j ∈ s, g j • v j⟫ := by
    rw [inner_sum]
    symm
    convert Finset.sum_eq_single (M := 𝕜) i ?_ ?_
    · rw [inner_smul_right]
    · intro j _hj hji
      rw [inner_smul_right, ho hji.symm, mul_zero]
    · exact fun h => False.elim (h hi)
  simpa [hg, hz] using h'

applications.title: Certify independence through orthogonality
applications.inputs: Use v1=(1,1,0), v2=(1,-1,0), v3=(0,0,2) in R^3 with the usual dot product.
applications.hypotheses: The Euclidean inner product has a separating norm. The theorem requires each vector nonzero and each pair orthogonal.

steps.text: The first two vectors have dot product 1-1+0=0.
The dot product of the third vector (0,0,2) with the first vector (1,1,0) is 0*1+0*1+2*0, which is 0 because the third coordinate of the first vector vanishes.
The dot product of the third vector (0,0,2) with the second vector (1,-1,0) is 0*1+0*(-1)+2*0, which is 0 for the same reason.
The squared norms of the first two vectors are both 2, so neither vector is zero.
The third vector has squared norm 4 and is therefore nonzero. All pairwise orthogonality conditions now hold.
Apply the orthogonal-independence theorem. A finite relation c1 v1+c2 v2+c3 v3=0 must have every coefficient zero.

applications.conclusion: The 3 vectors are linearly independent. The certificate uses 3 dot products and positive squared norms, without row reduction.

results.name: norm_eq_sqrt_re_inner
results.statement: For every x in an inner product space, N(x)=sqrt(real part of <x,x>).
hypotheses: V is a real or complex inner product space. The first slot is conjugate-linear and the second is linear. The norm satisfies N(x)^2=<x,x>.

proof.verification: complete readable proof; agent review required; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Norm compatibility gives real part of <x,x>=N(x)^2. The norm is a nonnegative real number.
The nonnegative square root of the square of a nonnegative real t is t by the definition of square root. Substitute t=N(x).

theorem norm_eq_sqrt_re_inner (x : E) : ‖x‖ = √(re ⟪x, x⟫) :=
  calc
    ‖x‖ = √(‖x‖ ^ 2) := (sqrt_sq (norm_nonneg _)).symm
    _ = √(re ⟪x, x⟫) := congr_arg _ (norm_sq_eq_re_inner _)

results.statement: If v,w are orthogonal in a real or complex inner product space, then N(w-v)=N(w+v).

results.name: Polynomial.root_or_root_of_root_mul
results.statement: In an integral domain R, a root a of pq is a root of p or a root of q.
hypotheses: R is a commutative integral domain. p,q are polynomials over R and a belongs to R. Evaluation of pq at a is 0.

proof.verification: complete readable proof; agent review required; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Multiplicative evaluation with the identity coefficient map gives (pq)(a)=p(a)q(a). The root assumption therefore gives p(a)q(a)=0.
An integral domain has no zero divisors, so p(a)=0 or q(a)=0. These are exactly the two root alternatives.

prerequisites.reason: The root of the product gives a product of scalar evaluations equal to 0.

  | n + 1 =>

      _ ≤ (n + 1) * (n + 1) ^ n := Nat.mul_le_mul_left _ (Nat.pow_le_pow_left n.le_succ _)

results.name: Nat.ascFactorial_mul_ascFactorial
results.statement: For natural n,l,k, the product of l consecutive factors from n times the product of k consecutive factors from n+l equals the product of l+k consecutive factors from n.
hypotheses: n,l,k are natural numbers. The ascending factorial n^(over r) is the product n(n+1)...(n+r-1), with the empty product equal to 1.

proof.verification: complete readable proof; agent review required; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: The first product contains factors n through n+l-1. The second contains factors n+l through n+l+k-1. These two adjacent ranges concatenate to the range of l+k factors.
Associativity of multiplication identifies the product of the two finite products with the product over the concatenated range. Empty ranges follow from the identity factor 1.

source.excerpt:
theorem ascFactorial_mul_ascFactorial (n l k : ℕ) :
    n.ascFactorial l * (n + l).ascFactorial k = n.ascFactorial (l + k) := by
  cases n with
  | zero =>
    cases l
    · simp only [ascFactorial_zero, Nat.add_zero, Nat.one_mul, Nat.zero_add]
    · simp only [Nat.add_right_comm, zero_ascFactorial, Nat.zero_add, Nat.zero_mul]
  | succ n' =>
    apply Nat.mul_left_cancel (factorial_pos n')
    simp only [Nat.add_assoc, ← Nat.mul_assoc, factorial_mul_ascFactorial]
    rw [Nat.add_comm 1 l, ← Nat.add_assoc, factorial_mul_ascFactorial, Nat.add_assoc]

results.name: Nat.choose_mul_factorial_mul_factorial
results.statement: For natural k<=n, C(n,k) k! (n-k)!=n!.
hypotheses: n,k,s,i,j are natural numbers. C(n,k) is the number of k-element subsets of an n-element set. It equals 0 when k>n. The empty subset gives C(n,0)=1.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: An n-element set has n! orderings: the empty set has 1 ordering, and a nonempty set chooses its first element and orders the rest. Induction with the factorial recurrence gives this count.
An ordering determines its first k elements as an unordered subset S. Conversely, choose S, order its k elements, and order the remaining n-k elements. Concatenation recovers a unique ordering.
This is a bijection between orderings and these three independent choices. Their counts are C(n,k), k! and (n-k)!. Multiplication of finite counts proves the identity, including k=0 and k=n.

prerequisites.reason: The recurrence counts orderings by the choice of their first element.

theorem choose_mul_factorial_mul_factorial : ∀ {n k}, k ≤ n → choose n k * k ! * (n - k)! = n !
  | 0, _, hk => by simp [Nat.eq_zero_of_le_zero hk]
  | n + 1, 0, _ => by simp
  | n + 1, succ k, hk => by
    rcases lt_or_eq_of_le hk with hk₁ | hk₁
    · have h : choose n k * k.succ ! * (n - k)! = (k + 1) * n ! := by
        rw [← choose_mul_factorial_mul_factorial (le_of_succ_le_succ hk)]
        simp [factorial_succ, Nat.mul_comm, Nat.mul_left_comm, Nat.mul_assoc]
      have h₁ : (n - k)! = (n - k) * (n - k.succ)! := by
        rw [← succ_sub_succ, succ_sub (le_of_lt_succ hk₁), factorial_succ]
      have h₂ : choose n (succ k) * k.succ ! * ((n - k) * (n - k.succ)!) = (n - k) * n ! := by
        rw [← choose_mul_factorial_mul_factorial (le_of_lt_succ hk₁)]
        simp [factorial_succ, Nat.mul_comm, Nat.mul_left_comm, Nat.mul_assoc]
      have h₃ : k * n ! ≤ n * n ! := Nat.mul_le_mul_right _ (le_of_succ_le_succ hk)
      rw [choose_succ_succ, Nat.add_mul, Nat.add_mul, succ_sub_succ, h, h₁, h₂, Nat.add_mul,
        Nat.mul_sub_right_distrib, factorial_succ, ← Nat.add_sub_assoc h₃, Nat.add_assoc,
        ← Nat.add_mul, Nat.add_sub_cancel_left, Nat.add_comm]
    · rw [hk₁]; simp [Nat.mul_comm, choose, Nat.sub_self]

results.name: Nat.choose_mul
results.statement: For natural s<=k, C(n,k) C(k,s)=C(n,s) C(n-s,k-s).
hypotheses: n,k,s,i,j are natural numbers. C(n,k) is the number of k-element subsets of an n-element set. It equals 0 when k>n. The empty subset gives C(n,0)=1.

proof.verification: complete readable proof; agent review required; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Count pairs of subsets S subset T of a fixed n-element set with sizes s,k. First choose T, then S inside T. This gives C(n,k) C(k,s) pairs.
Alternatively choose S, then choose k-s additional elements from its complement of size n-s. This gives C(n,s) C(n-s,k-s) pairs.

Both methods enumerate the same finite pairs bijectively, so their counts are equal. If k>n, there are no such pairs. If also s>n, both counts vanish. If s<=n<k, then k-s>n-s and the second factor on the right vanishes.

source.excerpt:
theorem choose_mul {n k s : ℕ} (hsk : s ≤ k) :
    n.choose k * k.choose s = n.choose s * (n - s).choose (k - s) := by
  obtain hnk | hkn := lt_or_ge n k
  · grind
  have h : 0 < (n - k)! * (k - s)! * s ! := by apply_rules [factorial_pos, Nat.mul_pos]
  apply Nat.mul_right_cancel h
  calc
    _ = n.choose s * s ! * ((n - s).choose (k - s) * (k - s)! * (n - s - (k - s))!) := by
      grind [choose_mul_factorial_mul_factorial]
    _ = n.choose s * (n - s).choose (k - s) * ((n - k)! * (k - s)! * s !) := by
      grind

results.name: Nat.add_choose
results.statement: For natural i,j, C(i+j,j)=(i+j)!/(i! j!), with exact integer division.
hypotheses: n,k,s,i,j are natural numbers. C(n,k) is the number of k-element subsets of an n-element set. It equals 0 when k>n. The empty subset gives C(n,0)=1.
All indices are natural numbers, including 0 unless an additional inequality excludes it. Factorial n! is the product of integers from 1 to n, with 0!=1.

proof.verification: complete readable proof; agent review required; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: The factorial coefficient identity with n=i+j and k=j gives C(i+j,j) j! i!=(i+j)!.

Factorials are positive, so the denominator i! j! is nonzero. Division of this integer multiple by its positive factor gives exactly C(i+j,j). Commutativity of multiplication puts the denominator in the displayed order.

prerequisites.reason: The factorial identity supplies the exact multiple.
The divisor is positive and permits exact cancellation.

    Nat.mul_comm]

results.name: Nat.choose_le_middle
results.statement: For all natural n,r, C(n,r)<=C(n,floor(n/2)).
hypotheses: n,k,s,i,j are natural numbers. C(n,k) is the number of k-element subsets of an n-element set. It equals 0 when k>n. The empty subset gives C(n,0)=1.
All indices are natural numbers, including 0 unless an additional inequality excludes it. Factorial n! is the product of integers from 1 to n, with 0!=1.

proof.verification: complete readable proof; agent review required; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: If r>n, the left count is 0, so the bound follows from nonnegativity. Assume r<=n. The factorial identity gives C(n,j)=n!/(j!(n-j)!) for all j<=n, since both denominator factors are positive.
For j<n, cancellation in this formula gives C(n,j+1)=C(n,j)(n-j)/(j+1). If j<floor(n/2), then n-j>=j+1, so C(n,j+1)>=C(n,j). All divisions here have positive denominators.

If r<=floor(n/2), repeat this inequality from r to the middle. If r>floor(n/2), replace r by n-r, which is at most the middle. The factorial formula gives C(n,r)=C(n,n-r) by exchange of the two denominator factors.
The preceding increasing sequence bound now applies to n-r. Thus every r has the stated bound, including n=0.

prerequisites.reason: The proof derives the coefficient ratio and reflection identity from the factorial formula.
The factorial denominators are positive.

source.excerpt:
theorem choose_le_middle (r n : ℕ) : choose n r ≤ choose n (n / 2) := by
  rcases le_or_gt r n with b | b
  · rcases le_or_gt r (n / 2) with a | h
    · apply choose_le_middle_of_le_half_left a
    · rw [← choose_symm b]
      apply choose_le_middle_of_le_half_left
      lia
  · rw [choose_eq_zero_of_lt b]
    apply zero_le

applications.title: Find the largest layer of subsets of a 10-element set
applications.inputs: A set has 10 distinct elements. Its rank-r layer consists of all subsets with exactly r elements.
applications.hypotheses: The binomial middle-layer theorem applies with n=10 and any natural r.

steps.text: The middle index is floor(10/2)=5. The factorial formula gives C(10,5)=10!/(5!5!).
For comparison, the neighboring layer has C(10,4)=10!/(4!6!), with 4!=24 and 6!=720.
The theorem proves C(10,r)<=C(10,5)=252 for every r. It covers all layers without individual enumeration.

applications.conclusion: A middle layer contains 252 subsets and has at least as many subsets as every other rank layer.

results.name: Nat.multichoose_eq
results.statement: For natural n,k, the number of multisets of size k from n types equals C(n+k-1,k), with natural subtraction in the upper index.
hypotheses: n,k,s,i,j are natural numbers. C(n,k) is the number of k-element subsets of an n-element set. It equals 0 when k>n. The empty subset gives C(n,0)=1.
A multiset records a nonnegative multiplicity for each of n types, with total multiplicity k.

proof.verification: complete readable proof; agent review required; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: If k=0, there is exactly 1 empty multiset and C(n-1,0)=1, including n=0. If n=0 and k>0, no such multiset exists and C(k-1,k)=0.
For n>=1 and k>=1, write each multiset uniquely as a nondecreasing sequence 1<=a1<=...<=ak<=n. Map it to the strict sequence b_t=a_t+t-1 for t=1,...,k. These indices satisfy 1<=b1<...<bk<=n+k-1.
Conversely, from such a strict sequence set a_t=b_t-t+1. The strict index spacing gives nondecreasing a_t and a_t>=1. Since b_t<=n+k-1-(k-t), it gives a_t<=n.
These transformations are inverse. Strict sequences correspond to k-element subsets of an (n+k-1)-element set, whose count is C(n+k-1,k). This proves the formula in every case.

prerequisites.reason: The worked application converts the subset count into an exact factorial quotient.
The factorial quotient has a positive denominator.

source.excerpt:
theorem multichoose_eq : ∀ n k : ℕ, multichoose n k = (n + k - 1).choose k
  | _, 0 => by simp
  | 0, k + 1 => by simp
  | n + 1, k + 1 => by
    have : n + (k + 1) < (n + 1) + (k + 1) := Nat.add_lt_add_right (Nat.lt_succ_self _) _
    have : (n + 1) + k < (n + 1) + (k + 1) := Nat.add_lt_add_left (Nat.lt_succ_self _) _
    rw [multichoose_succ_succ, Nat.add_comm, Nat.succ_add_sub_one, ← Nat.add_assoc,
      Nat.choose_succ_succ]
    simp [multichoose_eq n (k + 1), multichoose_eq (n + 1) k]

applications.title: Distribute 7 identical items among 4 labeled bins
applications.inputs: There are 4 labeled bins and 7 indistinguishable items. Each bin may contain any nonnegative number of items.
applications.hypotheses: The multiplicities have total 7. Empty bins are permitted. The theorem applies with n=4 and k=7.

steps.text: Stars and bars maps the 4 multiplicities to a 7-element subset of a set with 4+7-1=10 positions. The bijection in the proof includes empty bins.
The factorial coefficient identity gives C(10,7)=10!/(7!3!). The recurrence gives 10!=3628800, 7!=5040 and 3!=6.

applications.conclusion: There are exactly 120 distributions, including those with one or more empty bins.

results.name: Pascal recurrence for binomial coefficients
results.statement: For every natural n,k, C(n+1,k+1)=C(n,k)+C(n,k+1).
hypotheses: n,k,s,i,j are natural numbers. C(n,k) is the number of k-element subsets of an n-element set. It equals 0 when k>n. The empty subset gives C(n,0)=1.

proof.verification: complete readable proof; agent review required; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Fix one distinguished element in an (n+1)-element set. Partition its (k+1)-element subsets according to whether they contain that element.
Subsets that contain it correspond bijectively, by removal of that element, to k-element subsets of the other n elements. Subsets that exclude it are (k+1)-element subsets of those n elements.
The two classes are disjoint and exhaust all subsets. Their counts add, giving the recurrence. This holds also for indices outside range because the relevant classes are empty.
